chemicals.concentration_notes: A single stick of sugar-free gum can contain up to 1 gram of xylitol. This is enough to poison a small dog, but cats tolerated doses up to 1,000 mg/kg with no toxic effects.
chemicals.description: Xylitol is the artificial sweetener in sugar-free gum. It is not toxic to cats. The ASPCA states that people, cats, and ferrets are not negatively affected by xylitol, and a 2018 study found cats had no change in blood sugar, no liver damage, and only transient drooling. The severe insulin surge, hypoglycaemia, and liver failure caused by xylitol are specific to dogs and do not occur in cats.
chemicals.name: Xylitol (Artificial Sweetener)

chemicals.concentration_notes: Even a single swallowed piece of gum can pose a choking hazard or cause a gastrointestinal blockage in a small animal like a cat.
chemicals.description: Standard sugary gum and the gum base itself are not chemically toxic, but they present a physical danger. Swallowed chewing gum cannot be broken down by the feline digestive system and can act as a foreign body, potentially causing an obstruction or blockage in the esophagus, stomach, or intestines.
chemicals.name: Indigestible Gum Base (Physical Hazard)

description:
Chewing gum is not chemically toxic to cats, but a swallowed piece can still cause problems. The main risk is mechanical: a wad of gum cannot be digested and may cause choking or a gastrointestinal blockage, especially in a small cat.

Many people worry about xylitol, the sweetener in sugar-free gum. Xylitol is genuinely dangerous to dogs, but authorities including the ASPCA state that cats are not negatively affected by it. A 2018 study gave cats doses up to 1,000 mg/kg with no drop in blood sugar, no liver damage, and only brief drooling. So the chemical poisoning seen in dogs does not apply to cats.

There is still no reason to let a cat eat gum. If a cat swallows gum, watch for drooling, vomiting, reduced appetite, or signs of an obstruction such as repeated retching or straining, and contact a veterinarian if these appear. Keep gum out of reach to avoid the choking and blockage risk.
emergencyNote: Cats are not poisoned by xylitol, so a chemical emergency is not expected. The real concern is a swallowed gum mass causing choking or a gastrointestinal blockage. Contact a veterinarian if a cat shows repeated retching, straining, vomiting, or lethargy after swallowing gum.
name: Gum
safetyNotes: Main hazard is mechanical, not chemical: a swallowed gum wad is indigestible and can cause choking or a gastrointestinal blockage, especially in a small cat

Xylitol is NOT toxic to cats: the ASPCA states people, cats, and ferrets are not negatively affected by xylitol, and a 2018 study found no hypoglycaemia or liver damage in cats at doses up to 1,000 mg/kg
The severe hypoglycaemia and liver failure caused by xylitol are a dog-specific risk and do not apply to cats
Signs to watch for after a cat swallows gum: brief drooling, vomiting, reduced appetite, or signs of obstruction such as repeated retching, straining, or lethargy
Keep gum and breath mints out of reach to prevent choking and blockage; contact a veterinarian if obstruction signs appear

symptoms.name: Transient Salivation (Drooling)
symptoms.notes: In a 2018 experimental study where cats were given oral doses of xylitol up to 1,000 mg/kg, the cats exhibited no changes in blood glucose, liver enzymes, or hematological parameters. The animals remained well, with transient salivation being the only reported clinical sign.

symptoms.name: Gastrointestinal Upset or Obstruction
symptoms.notes: The indigestible gum base cannot be broken down and can act as a foreign body, potentially causing a physical gastrointestinal obstruction. Watch for vomiting, repeated retching, straining, or reduced appetite.

treatments.description: Because xylitol does not poison cats, treatment focuses on the mechanical risk. Identify how much gum was swallowed and whether the cat is showing any signs of choking or obstruction.
treatments.name: Assess for Choking or Obstruction Risk
treatments.notes: No antidote or hypoglycaemia treatment is needed for the xylitol itself in cats; the concern is a swallowed gum mass acting as a foreign body.

treatments.description: of the procedure: If the gum was ingested very recently, the veterinarian will administer a specific injection to make the cat vomit, emptying the stomach to minimize the absorption of any potential toxins.
treatments.name: Early Gastrointestinal Decontamination
treatments.notes: This procedure is only helpful if performed very quickly after ingestion; it is too late to induce vomiting if symptoms have already developed7. Pet owners should never attempt to induce vomiting at home, as there are no safe methods for doing so in cats without professional veterinary care.

treatments.description: If a swallowed gum mass causes a gastrointestinal blockage, the veterinarian may use imaging to locate it and, if needed, remove it endoscopically or surgically. Cats do not require hypoglycaemia treatment for xylitol.
treatments.name: Obstruction Management (If Blockage Develops)
treatments.notes: Watch for repeated retching, straining, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, or lethargy, which can indicate an obstruction and warrant prompt veterinary care.

treatments.description: of the procedure: The veterinarian will run blood tests to confirm blood glucose levels and perform urinalysis. These tests help identify any instances of internal organ damage (such as liver impairment) and guide the ongoing treatment strategy610.
treatments.name: Diagnostic Testing and Ongoing Supportive Care
treatments.notes: In experimental studies where cats were given massive doses of xylitol (up to 1,000 mg/kg), their hematological and biochemical parameters remained unchanged111.
